name: Aye-aye
scope: T1 recognition of a wide-eyed nocturnal Madagascar lemur; the skeletal, elongated middle finger it taps on wood to find grubs (percussive foraging, ~8 taps/sec); how it hears the hollow echo of a larval tunnel with huge bat-like ears; then gnaws a hole with ever-growing rodent-like incisors and fishes the grub out with that same thin finger (a woodpecker's job done by a primate); the ball-and-socket wrist that lets the finger rotate freely; local Malagasy fady taboo treating it as an omen of death (coherent animal-anchored culture payoff).
source: Standard primatology references on Daubentonia madagascariensis (percussive foraging, ever-growing incisors, tap-scanning); Erickson studies on aye-aye tap-foraging.
framing_note: The animal is the anchor: every rung a fact about the aye-aye. Lead with the jaw-dropping skeletal tapping finger. One coherent wonder per rung — tap-scanning, echo-hearing, gnawing incisors, extracting finger, rotating wrist each get their OWN rung; never restate 'weird finger'. WONDER answers favor the VIVID ADAPTATION (the finger that taps and fishes) over generic labels. Accuracy: it fills the woodpecker niche on Madagascar (no woodpeckers there) — real convergence, state as ecology not anthropomorphism.

name: Slow loris
scope: T1 recognition of the huge-eyed, slow-moving Southeast Asian primate; the headline: the ONLY venomous primate — it raises its arms and licks a gland on the inside of its elbow (brachial gland), mixing the secretion with saliva to arm a toxic bite; the still-researched mechanism (the toxin resembles cat-allergen protein Fel d 1; envenomation can cause anaphylactic shock in humans, and lorises bite each other in fierce territorial fights); the tapetum that makes the eyes shine; the freeze-and-hang stillness as camouflage from predators.
source: Nekaris et al. research on Nycticebus venom (brachial gland, Fel d 1-like protein, conspecific bites); flag mechanism as active research.
framing_note: Anchor = the slow loris. Lead with 'only venomous primate.' RESEARCH-IN-PROGRESS FLAG (rule 5): the venom mechanism and the Fel d 1-similarity are genuine but still being studied — frame as 'what researchers have found' not settled fact; do NOT overstate the cat-allergen link as proven identity. One wonder per rung: arms-up delivery pose, the elbow gland, conspecific bite fights, eyeshine, freeze-camouflage each own a rung. No anthropomorphizing.

name: Tarsier
scope: T1 recognition of the tiny Southeast Asian primate; the headline: each eyeball is bigger than its brain and cannot rotate in the socket — so it swivels its head nearly 180 degrees like an owl to look around; the fully carnivorous diet (the only entirely meat-eating primate — insects, lizards, even birds); the enormous ears and huge leaping hind limbs (named for elongated tarsal ankle bones); ultrasonic calls above human hearing.
source: Primatology references on Tarsiidae (eye-to-brain size, immobile eyes, head rotation, obligate carnivory, ultrasonic calls).
framing_note: Anchor = the tarsier. Lead with 'eyes bigger than its brain.' The eyes-can't-move fact and the owl-like head swivel are ONE coherent wonder (the head turns BECAUSE the eyes can't) — keep them in one rung or split cleanly into cause/effect. Separate rungs: obligate carnivory (the only all-meat primate), ultrasonic calls, ankle-bone leaping. WONDER answer = the vivid fact (eyeball bigger than brain), not a number for its own sake.

name: Proboscis monkey
scope: T1 recognition of the Borneo monkey with the pendulous nose; the headline: the male's huge drooping nose acts as a resonating chamber, amplifying his honking call and (females prefer bigger noses) advertising fitness; the potbelly holding a chambered, foregut-fermenting stomach full of bacteria to digest leaves and unripe fruit (ripe fruit can ferment and bloat them dangerously); webbed feet and belly-flop swimming — among the best-swimming monkeys, crossing rivers to escape crocodiles.
source: Primatology references on Nasalis larvatus (nose as resonator + sexual selection, foregut fermentation, swimming/webbed feet).
framing_note: Anchor = the proboscis monkey. Lead with the resonating nose. One wonder per rung: nose-as-loudspeaker, foregut fermentation belly, webbed-foot river swimming. The nose is the headline — do NOT restate it; the fermentation and swimming are distinct wonders. Sexual-selection framing = 'females prefer / the nose advertises' as ecology, not human romance.

name: Okapi
scope: T1 recognition of the Congo forest animal with zebra-striped legs; the headline reveal: it is NOT related to zebras — it is the giraffe's only living relative (short-necked forest cousin), unknown to Western science until 1901 (the 'African unicorn'); the ~30 cm prehensile blue-black tongue long enough to lick its own eyes and ears clean; the striped rump as dazzle-camouflage in dappled forest light and a follow-me signal for calves.
source: References on Okapia johnstoni (giraffe relative, 1901 description, prehensile tongue, striping function).
framing_note: Anchor = the okapi. Lead with the twist: stripes say zebra, but it's the giraffe's cousin. Distinct rungs: giraffe kinship (headline), the eye-cleaning tongue, the dazzle-stripe function, the 1901 discovery (coherent human-drama payoff — a real 'hidden giant' story, not orphan trivia). Do NOT restate 'stripes' as the answer twice.

name: Saiga antelope
scope: T1 recognition of the Central Asian steppe antelope with the bulbous trunk-like nose; the headline: the oversized flexible nose filters out dust from summer dust-storms and warms freezing winter air before it reaches the lungs; the mass migrations across the steppe; the 2015 catastrophe when a bacterium (Pasteurella multocida) normally harmless suddenly killed ~200,000 saiga in weeks when heat and humidity spiked (animal-anchored payoff on why it was vulnerable).
source: References on Saiga tatarica (nasal air-conditioning/filtering, 2015 mass mortality Pasteurella event).
framing_note: Anchor = the saiga. Lead with the bizarre air-conditioning nose. Distinct rungs: dust-filtering nose (headline), warming-winter-air function (a DIFFERENT job of the same nose = fine as a second coherent rung if framed as a distinct fact), migration, the 2015 die-off (coherent 'why it was vulnerable' payoff, per the topic-list reframing of extinctions/threats). Keep the die-off animal-anchored, not a conservation-policy lecture.

name: Babirusa
scope: T1 recognition of the near-hairless Indonesian 'deer-pig'; the headline: the male's upper canines grow UP through the top of the snout, piercing the skin and curving back toward its own forehead — and if never worn down they can curl round and grow into the animal's own skull; the four tusks total (lower pair also curve up); the wallowing and multi-chambered stomach hinting at a ruminant-like gut unusual for a pig.
source: References on Babyrousa (upward-piercing canines through the snout, potential self-impaling growth, unusual stomach).
framing_note: Anchor = the babirusa. Lead with the tusks that grow up through the snout toward the skull. That IS the headline — the 'curl into its own skull' is the same wonder's climax; give it one rung, don't pad. The four-tusk count and the odd stomach are the additional distinct rungs. Mini depth: thin beats fabricated.

name: Pink fairy armadillo
scope: T1 recognition of the tiny (~10 cm) pink-shelled Argentine armadillo; the headline: it 'swims' through sand — a sand-swimming burrower that spends nearly all its life underground; the pink shell is thin and translucent because blood vessels beneath it flush warm or cool to regulate temperature; the flat, vertical armored butt-plate it uses to tamp soil behind it, sealing its tunnel like a cork.
source: References on Chlamyphorus truncatus (sand-swimming, vascularized thermoregulating carapace, rear butt-plate for tunnel sealing).
framing_note: Anchor = the pink fairy armadillo. Lead with sand-swimming. Distinct rungs: sand-swimming (headline), the blood-flushing pink shell as a radiator, the rear armor plate that tamps and seals the burrow. Do NOT restate 'small pink armadillo.' Thin ladder honest to how little is known (it's rarely seen) — mini depth.

name: Solenodon
scope: T1 recognition of the shrew-like Caribbean 'living fossil'; the headline: it is one of very few venomous mammals — it delivers toxic saliva through a groove in its second lower incisor (a snake-like grooved-tooth delivery, rare in mammals); the lineage split from other mammals ~70+ million years ago, surviving the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs; a ball-and-socket joint at the base of its long flexible snout (unique among mammals).
source: References on Solenodon (grooved venom-delivering incisor, ancient lineage predating K-Pg, ball-and-socket snout).
framing_note: Anchor = the solenodon. Lead with venom through a grooved tooth (the name literally means 'grooved tooth'). Distinct rungs: grooved-tooth venom delivery (headline), the ancient lineage that outlived the dinosaurs (coherent deep-time payoff), the ball-and-socket snout. Accuracy: venomous mammals are genuinely rare — state which few share the trait (e.g. solenodon, some shrews, platypus, slow loris) without overclaiming.

name: Tasmanian devil
scope: T1 recognition of the black, screeching marsupial scavenger; the headline: pound-for-pound one of the strongest mammal bites, jaws that can crush and eat bone and all (skull, fur, teeth); the blood-curdling nighttime screech that named it a 'devil'; the contagious facial tumor (DFTD) — a rare transmissible cancer spread by biting during feeding and fighting (coherent 'why it was vulnerable' payoff); newborns the size of a grain of rice racing to the pouch.
source: References on Sarcophilus harrisii (bite force/bone-crushing, screech, DFTD transmissible cancer, marsupial birth).
framing_note: Anchor = the Tasmanian devil. Lead with the bone-crushing bite. Distinct rungs: bite/bone-eating (headline), the screech, the transmissible face cancer (a genuinely astonishing biology fact — a cancer that spreads like an infection via bites; keep animal-anchored, framed as biology, not a conservation sermon), rice-grain newborn pouch race. One wonder per rung.

name: Quokka
scope: T1 recognition of the small round-faced Australian marsupial famous for looking like it's smiling; the headline: the 'smile' is just the shape of its face (a caution against reading human emotion into an animal — teachable accuracy moment); it can throw its own joey from the pouch as a decoy to distract a predator while it escapes; it recycles water and survives long dry spells on Rottnest Island; it can climb small trees and shrubs, unusual for a wallaby-relative.
source: References on Setonix brachyurus (facial morphology not emotion, joey-ejection anti-predator behavior, arid-island water conservation).
framing_note: Anchor = the quokka. Lead with 'the world's happiest-looking animal' hook — then the wonder is the CORRECTION: the smile is anatomy, not a mood (bakes in rule 5's no-anthropomorphizing-as-fact directly into the lesson). Distinct rungs: face-shape-not-emotion (headline), joey-decoy escape, arid water recycling. Do NOT present the smile as real happiness.

name: Lowland streaked tenrec
scope: T1 recognition of the tiny quilled black-and-yellow Madagascar insectivore; the headline: it rubs specialized quills on its back together to make ultrasonic clicks — stridulation, like a cricket, the only mammal known to communicate this way; the barbed detachable quills it drives into a predator's face; the huge Madagascar tenrec radiation (one ancestor evolving into shrew-, hedgehog-, otter- and mole-like forms).
source: References on Hemicentetes semispinosus (stridulation via quills — unique among mammals, barbed defensive quills, tenrec adaptive radiation).
framing_note: Anchor = the streaked tenrec. Lead with 'the mammal that buzzes like an insect' (quill stridulation). Distinct rungs: stridulation communication (headline), barbed defensive quills, the tenrec radiation on Madagascar. The insect-like sound is the headline — the defense and the radiation are the other two coherent wonders. Mini depth.

name: Fossa
scope: T1 recognition of Madagascar's top predator, a cat-like carnivore that isn't a cat; the headline reveal: it's a euplerid, closest to the mongoose family, that evolved cat-like hunting on Madagascar (convergence); semi-retractable claws and reversible ankles that let it run headfirst DOWN tree trunks to chase lemurs; its main prey is lemurs, making it the island's apex hunter.
source: References on Cryptoprocta ferox (euplerid/mongoose kinship not felid, reversible ankles + headfirst descent, lemur predation as apex predator).
framing_note: Anchor = the fossa. Lead with 'Madagascar's cat that isn't a cat.' Distinct rungs: mongoose-kin-not-cat (headline convergence twist), the reversible ankles for running down trees headfirst, apex-lemur-hunter role. Do NOT restate 'looks like a cat.' Mini depth — thin honest ladder.

name: Binturong
scope: T1 recognition of the shaggy black Southeast Asian 'bearcat' (neither bear nor cat, a viverrid); the headline: it smells strongly of hot buttered popcorn — the scent compound is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (2-AP), the very molecule that makes popcorn and jasmine rice smell the way they do, produced in its urine and used to scent-mark territory; the fully prehensile tail (one of only two Old World mammals with a truly grasping tail) used as a fifth limb in the canopy; reversible hind feet for climbing down headfirst.
source: Greene et al. 2016 identifying 2-AP in binturong urine; references on Arctictis binturong prehensile tail and reversible ankles.
framing_note: Anchor = the binturong. Lead with the buttered-popcorn smell. RESEARCH FLAG (rule 5): the 2-AP identification is real and published (Greene 2016) — state the molecule as the researched finding; the WONDER answer is the vivid handle 'the same molecule that makes popcorn smell like popcorn,' not the bare chemical name in isolation. Distinct rungs: popcorn scent + 2-AP (headline), prehensile fifth-limb tail, reversible-foot headfirst descent.

name: Maned wolf
scope: T1 recognition of the tall red-gold South American canid on absurdly long legs; the headline reveal: it is NOT a wolf and NOT a fox — its own genus, the last of an ancient South American canine lineage, a 'fox on stilts' whose long legs let it see over tall grassland; its urine smells strongly of skunk/cannabis (the compound pyrazine), a long-range scent marker; it eats large amounts of a tomato-like fruit (the 'wolf apple,' Solanum lycocarpum) — a fruit-loving canid that helps disperse the seeds.
source: References on Chrysocyon brachyurus (own genus/lineage, long legs for grassland vision, pyrazine skunk-scent urine, wolf-apple fruit diet + seed dispersal).
framing_note: Anchor = the maned wolf. Lead with the stilts-legs 'not a wolf, not a fox' twist. Distinct rungs: long legs + solitary lineage (headline), skunk-smelling urine marker, the fruit-heavy diet and seed-dispersal role. Keep the fruit/seed-dispersal rung as animal ecology. One wonder per rung.

name: Red panda
scope: T1 recognition of the small russet bamboo-eater with the ringed tail; the headline: a 'false thumb' — an enlarged wrist bone (radial sesamoid) that works like an extra thumb to grip bamboo, evolved SEPARATELY from the giant panda's same trick (convergence between two bamboo-eaters); it's a carnivoran gut trying to live on bamboo, so it must eat huge amounts and moves slowly; the bushy ringed tail wrapped around itself as a cold-weather blanket in the Himalayan cold; it's its own family (Ailuridae), not a bear and not a raccoon.
source: References on Ailurus fulgens (radial-sesamoid false thumb, convergent with giant panda; carnivoran-on-bamboo digestion; own family Ailuridae).
framing_note: Anchor = the red panda. Lead with the false thumb. IMPORTANT convergence hook: the red panda and giant panda both grew a false thumb independently — but that comparison is best a red-panda rung framed as 'evolved separately.' Distinct rungs: false thumb (headline), carnivore-gut-on-bamboo problem, tail-as-blanket, own-family taxonomy. Don't restate 'eats bamboo' as an answer twice.

name: Giant panda
scope: T1 recognition of the black-and-white bamboo bear; the headline: its own 'false thumb,' an enlarged wrist bone (radial sesamoid) that lets it grip bamboo stalks — a real bear whose gut is still a carnivore's, so it must eat 12-14 hours a day and 12-38 kg of bamboo to survive; the digestive twist that it's genetically a carnivore (it even has the umami/meat-taste gene switched off, so bamboo tastes better); newborns astonishingly tiny — about 1/900th of the mother's weight, blind and pink.
source: References on Ailuropoda melanoleuca (radial-sesamoid pseudo-thumb; carnivoran digestive tract on bamboo; T1R1 umami-receptor pseudogene; tiny neonate ratio).
framing_note: Anchor = the giant panda. Lead with the false thumb (and note it's the SAME trick the red panda evolved separately — but keep the panda as the anchor here). Distinct rungs: false thumb (headline), carnivore-gut / eat-all-day problem, the disabled umami gene (astonishing: a bear that lost its taste for meat), the grain-of-butter-sized newborn. Accuracy: panda IS a bear (unlike red panda). One wonder per rung; do NOT repeat 'eats bamboo.'

name: Aardvark
scope: T1 recognition of the pig-snouted, rabbit-eared African ant-and-termite eater; the headline: it is so evolutionarily unique it is the sole survivor of its own order (Tubulidentata) — its closest relatives are elephants and manatees, not pigs or anteaters (convergent 'anteater' body); its teeth have no enamel and are made of thin tubes of dentine that keep growing; it digs a burrow so fast it can outdig several people, and its burrows shelter dozens of other species; it eats a fruit, the 'aardvark cucumber,' that grows underground and relies on the aardvark to dig it up and spread its seeds.
source: References on Orycteropus afer (order Tubulidentata, Afrotheria kinship, tubular enamel-less teeth, rapid burrowing + keystone burrows, aardvark-cucumber mutualism).
framing_note: Anchor = the aardvark. Lead with 'the only member of its whole order' + the surprise elephant/manatee kinship. Distinct rungs: sole-survivor order + Afrotheria kinship (headline), the tube-dentine ever-growing teeth (which name it), the fast keystone burrowing, the aardvark-cucumber mutualism. The anteater-like look is convergence, not kinship — teach that. One wonder per rung.

name: Numbat
scope: T1 recognition of the striped-backed Western Australian termite specialist; the headline: it is a marsupial that has almost NO functional teeth and eats up to ~20,000 termites a day, lapping them with a long sticky tongue; it is the only marsupial fully active by day (diurnal), timed to when termites are near the surface; the female has no pouch — the babies cling to exposed nipples under a patch of belly hair; it shelters in hollow logs and can plug the entrance with its tough rump.
source: References on Myrmecobius fasciatus (obligate termite diet ~20,000/day, diurnality unique among marsupials, absent pouch/exposed young, log-plugging rump).
framing_note: Anchor = the numbat. Lead with the termite-lapping tongue. Distinct rungs: termite specialist + long tongue (headline), the-only-daytime-marsupial (a genuinely surprising fact), the no-pouch exposed young, the rump-plugged log. WONDER answers = vivid facts; the '~20,000 termites' is a constructed, evocative number (rule 4), acceptable as a scene handle, not a cold stat.

name: Musk ox
scope: T1 recognition of the shaggy Arctic tundra ox with the sweeping horns; the headline: its defense is a circle — when wolves attack, the herd forms a ring with horns facing out and the calves hidden inside; its undercoat, qiviut, is warmer than sheep's wool and finer than cashmere, shed in spring so the animal survives -40 winters; the massive horn boss across the forehead that bulls slam together head-on at high speed in the rut; it survived the ice age that killed the mammoth (coherent 'why it endured' payoff).
source: References on Ovibos moschatus (defensive ring formation, qiviut insulation, horn-boss head-clashing rut, ice-age relict survival).
framing_note: Anchor = the musk ox. Lead with the defensive ring against wolves. Distinct rungs: the horn-out ring (headline), qiviut super-wool, the head-slamming horn boss, ice-age survival. One coherent wonder per rung. Keep the ice-age-survivor rung animal-anchored (why THIS animal made it through), per the topic-list reframing.

name: Capybara
scope: T1 recognition of the giant South American rodent; the headline: it is the world's largest rodent, dog-plus-sized, with ever-growing rodent incisors; it's semi-aquatic — eyes, ears and nostrils set high on the head so it can stay submerged with just the top showing, and it can hold its breath and hide underwater from predators; it re-eats its own soft morning droppings (coprophagy) to extract more nutrients from tough grass (like a rabbit); it's famously calm and lets many other animals rest on it.
source: References on Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris (largest rodent, semi-aquatic head placement + underwater hiding, coprophagy/hindgut fermentation, social tolerance).
framing_note: Anchor = the capybara. Lead with 'biggest rodent in the world.' Distinct rungs: largest-rodent + ever-growing teeth (headline), the high-set eyes/ears/nose for near-total submersion (a DIFFERENT wonder from just being big), the re-eaten morning droppings for digestion. Keep the 'calm, everyone sits on it' as ecology/behavior, not a meme. One wonder per rung.

name: Kangaroo rat
scope: T1 recognition of the tiny hopping desert rodent of the American Southwest; the headline: it can live its entire life without ever drinking water — it makes 'metabolic water' from the dry seeds it eats and its ultra-efficient kidneys produce urine so concentrated it's nearly a paste; it never sweats and blocks water loss with elaborate nasal passages that recapture moisture from each breath; it hops on two legs like a kangaroo and can leap ~9x its body length to dodge a striking rattlesnake, sometimes kicking sand in the snake's face.
source: References on Dipodomys (metabolic water from seeds, ultra-concentrating kidneys, nasal countercurrent moisture recapture, bipedal escape leaps + snake-kicking).
framing_note: Anchor = the kangaroo rat. Lead with 'never drinks water in its life.' Distinct rungs: metabolic water / super-kidneys (headline), the moisture-recapturing nose and no-sweat body (a distinct part of the water story — frame as its own mechanism rung), the bipedal snake-dodging leap. Note this animal overlaps the 'living without water' adaptation ladder — this creature ladder deepens the kangaroo rat specifically.

name: Kakapo
scope: T1 recognition of the large moss-green New Zealand parrot; the headline: it is the world's only flightless parrot AND the heaviest, a nocturnal ground-dweller; the male's mating call is a deep 'boom' he makes by inflating an air sac in his chest, digging a bowl to amplify it, booming through the night — a lek where females walk in from kilometers away; it froze still as its anti-predator instinct, which worked against hawks but doomed it against introduced cats and stoats (coherent 'why it was vulnerable' payoff); it can live for decades and breeds only in years when the rimu tree fruits heavily.
source: References on Strigops habroptilus (only flightless/heaviest parrot, booming lek display + bowl amplifier, freeze instinct maladaptive to mammals, mast-driven breeding).
framing_note: Anchor = the kakapo. Lead with 'the only parrot that can't fly.' Distinct rungs: flightless/heaviest parrot (headline), the inflating-chest boom + dug bowl lek, the freeze-instinct that backfired against introduced mammals (animal-anchored vulnerability, not a conservation-org story), the rimu-mast breeding trigger. One wonder per rung.

name: Kea
scope: T1 recognition of the olive-green New Zealand alpine parrot; the headline: it's a mountain parrot with striking problem-solving intelligence — keas solve multi-step puzzles, use and share tools, and work together to get food (cooperative problem-solving rare in birds); its notorious curiosity and destructiveness — it pries rubber from car windshields and backpacks apart out of sheer investigative play; experiments show keas can grasp probability, choosing the better odds — a level of statistical reasoning seen in few animals.
source: References on Nestor notabilis (tool use + cooperative puzzle-solving, object-play/destructiveness, statistical-inference experiments Bastos & Taylor 2020).
framing_note: Anchor = the kea. Lead with 'the alpine parrot that solves puzzles.' Distinct rungs: puzzle-solving/tool cooperation (headline), the mischievous object-destroying curiosity, the probability-reasoning experiment (a concrete, jaw-dropping cognition result — keep it as the animal's demonstrated ability, not overstated as human-level). One wonder per rung.

name: Hoatzin
scope: T1 recognition of the spiky-crested Amazon river bird; the headline: its chicks are born with functional CLAWS on their wings — they scramble through branches and, if a predator threatens, drop into the water, swim, and climb back up using the wing-claws (an echo of Archaeopteryx, though not directly inherited); it is the only bird that digests leaves by fermenting them in an enlarged crop full of bacteria, like a cow's stomach — which makes it smell so bad locals call it the 'stinkbird'; the fermentation is slow, so it perches heavily and flies poorly.
source: References on Opisthocomus hoazin (juvenile wing-claws + water-escape climb, foregut leaf fermentation unique among birds, resulting odor).
framing_note: Anchor = the hoatzin. Lead with the chicks' wing-claws. Distinct rungs: wing-clawed swimming chicks (headline), the cow-like crop fermentation (a DIFFERENT wonder — the only foregut-fermenting bird), the 'stinkbird' smell as the coherent consequence of that fermentation. Accuracy: the wing-claws are a convergent/retained curiosity, NOT proof it descends from Archaeopteryx — frame carefully (rule 5).

name: Secretarybird
scope: T1 recognition of the tall, long-legged African raptor that hunts on foot; the headline: it kills snakes and prey by STOMPING — it strikes with its feet in about 15 milliseconds, faster than a blink, delivering forces many times its body weight to crush a snake's skull before the snake can bite back; it walks up to ~30 km a day hunting through grassland instead of soaring like most birds of prey; the crest of long quill-like head feathers that named it (said to look like quills tucked behind a clerk's ear); it stamps the ground to flush hidden prey.
source: References on Sagittarius serpentarius (kick-strike speed/force studies, terrestrial hunting range, crest feathers/naming, ground-stamping to flush prey).
framing_note: Anchor = the secretarybird. Lead with 'the eagle that kills snakes by stomping.' Distinct rungs: the ~15 ms killing kick (headline — the speed is a CONSTRUCTED, awe-making number, allowed by rule 4), the walk-to-hunt lifestyle, the quill-crest naming (coherent human-story payoff). One wonder per rung; don't restate 'stomps snakes.'

name: Frogmouth
scope: T1 recognition of the wide-mouthed Australian night bird (tawny frogmouth); the headline: it is a master of disguise — by day it stretches stiff, points its beak skyward, half-closes its eyes and freezes, so it looks EXACTLY like a broken branch stub; it is NOT an owl (it's related to nightjars) — it has a huge frog-like gape to snap up insects rather than an owl's talons; its cryptic bark-patterned plumage and stillness make it nearly invisible; it hunts by sitting and waiting, dropping onto prey below.
source: References on Podargus strigoides (broken-branch camouflage posture, nightjar kinship not owl, wide gape/sit-and-wait hunting).
framing_note: Anchor = the frogmouth. Lead with the broken-branch disguise pose. Distinct rungs: the branch-mimic freeze (headline), the not-an-owl reveal (nightjar kin, frog-mouth gape instead of talons), the sit-and-wait ambush. Pairs conceptually with the potoo but is its OWN ladder/animal. One wonder per rung.

name: Potoo
scope: T1 recognition of the huge-eyed Central/South American night bird; the headline: by day it perches bolt upright on a broken snag and becomes a dead stump — its camouflage is so total it looks like the tree itself; it has slits in its eyelids that let it detect movement and threats even with its eyes 'closed,' so it can stay frozen yet watchful; its enormous eyes gather faint light for catching insects on the wing at night; its mournful, ghostly wailing call gave rise to eerie folklore.
source: References on Nyctibius (dead-snag camouflage, eyelid 'magic slits' for vision while closed, large light-gathering eyes, haunting call).
framing_note: Anchor = the potoo. Lead with 'the bird that turns into a tree stump.' Distinct rungs: stump-mimic camouflage (headline), the eyelid slits that let it watch while 'asleep' (a genuinely uncanny, distinct wonder), the giant night-vision eyes. Keep DISTINCT from the frogmouth ladder — same theme, different animal/facts. The folklore-call can be a light payoff rung, animal-anchored.

name: Oilbird
scope: T1 recognition of the reddish-brown cave-dwelling South American night bird; the headline: it is one of the very few birds that ECHOLOCATE — it navigates pitch-black caves by making rapid clicking sounds and listening for the echoes, like a bat; it is entirely fruit-eating (unusual for a nocturnal bird), flying out at night to pluck oily palm and laurel fruits by hovering; the chicks grow so fat on oil-rich fruit that people once boiled them down for lamp oil, giving the bird its name (coherent animal-anchored payoff).
source: References on Steatornis caripensis (audible-click echolocation, frugivorous night foraging by hover, historical rendering of fat chicks for oil/naming).
framing_note: Anchor = the oilbird. Lead with 'a bird that echolocates like a bat.' Distinct rungs: click echolocation in caves (headline), the fruit-only night diet + hovering harvest, the oily-chick naming story (coherent human payoff, animal-anchored). Note it overlaps the echolocation adaptation ladder — this creature ladder deepens the oilbird itself. One wonder per rung.

name: Harpy eagle
scope: T1 recognition of the massive gray-and-black rainforest eagle with the double crest; the headline: its talons are as long as a grizzly bear's claws (~13 cm / 5 inches), the largest of any eagle, gripping with enough force to crush bone; it hunts by weaving through the canopy and snatching monkeys and sloths right off the branches, flying off carrying prey up to its own body weight; the facial disc of feathers it can raise to funnel sound to its ears (like an owl) to pinpoint prey; it raises just one chick every 2-3 years, a slow reproducer (coherent 'why it's vulnerable' payoff).
source: References on Harpia harpyja (talon size/grip force, canopy ambush of arboreal mammals, raisable facial disc for hearing, slow reproduction).
framing_note: Anchor = the harpy eagle. Lead with the bear-claw talons. Distinct rungs: talon size/grip (headline), the monkey-and-sloth snatch from the canopy, the sound-funneling facial disc, the slow one-chick reproduction (animal-anchored vulnerability). The talon length is a CONSTRUCTED comparison-number (as long as a bear's claws), allowed by rule 4. One wonder per rung.

name: Vulture
scope: T1 recognition of the bald-headed carrion bird circling on high; the headline: its stomach acid is so corrosive (near pH 0-1) it dissolves flesh, bone fragments and destroys anthrax, cholera and botulism bacteria that would kill other scavengers — a walking disease-disposal unit; the bald head is an adaptation, not ugliness — bare skin stays clean when the bird plunges into a carcass and lets it shed heat; some (turkey vultures) find carrion by SMELL, rare among birds, homing in on the gas of decay; it urinates on its own legs to cool down and to kill bacteria (urohidrosis).
source: References on New World & Old World vultures (extreme stomach acidity + pathogen destruction, bald-head hygiene/thermoregulation, olfactory carrion-finding in Cathartes, urohidrosis).
framing_note: Anchor = the vulture (treat as the vulture form — can specify turkey vulture for the smell rung). Lead with the acid-bath stomach. Distinct rungs: pathogen-killing acid gut (headline), the functional bald head, smell-based carrion finding, leg-urination cooling/disinfecting. Each is a DISTINCT wonder — do not restate 'eats dead things.' One wonder per rung.

name: Toucan
scope: T1 recognition of the rainforest bird with the enormous colorful bill; the headline: that huge bill is a living RADIATOR — the toucan pumps blood into it to dump body heat, adjusting the flow to shed or conserve warmth (one of the largest heat-exchange organs relative to body size in any animal); despite its size the bill is astonishingly light — a rigid foam of bony struts wrapped in keratin, so it barely weighs anything; the bill's reach lets the toucan sit still and pluck fruit from thin branches it couldn't perch on; at night it tucks the bill under a wing and folds its tail over its back to sleep as a compact ball.
source: References on Ramphastos (bill as thermoregulatory radiator, Tattersall et al. 2009; lightweight bony-strut/keratin structure; feeding reach; sleeping posture).
framing_note: Anchor = the toucan. Lead with 'the giant bill is a radiator.' Distinct rungs: heat-dumping bill (headline, Tattersall 2009 finding), the surprisingly featherlight foam-strut structure (a DIFFERENT wonder from its heat function), the reach-for-fruit advantage, the tuck-and-fold sleeping ball. One wonder per rung.

name: Superb bird-of-paradise
scope: T1 recognition of the New Guinea bird famous for its transforming courtship display; the headline: the courting male snaps open his black cape and iridescent blue-green breast shield into a perfect oval 'smiley face,' then hops around the female in a bouncing dance; his feathers are so structurally black (super-black) they absorb ~99.95% of light, so the blue face seems to glow against a void — one of the blackest materials in nature, made by microscopic feather structures not pigment; the female watches dozens of suitors and is extremely choosy; recent work split the display-and-dance form into its own species (Lophorina niedda).
source: References on Lophorina (smiley-face courtship transformation; super-black plumage absorbing ~99.95% light, McCoy et al. 2018; female choice; taxonomic split).
framing_note: Anchor = the superb bird-of-paradise. Lead with the smiley-face transformation dance. Distinct rungs: the oval-face display (headline), the super-black feathers that absorb almost all light (a distinct optical wonder — cite McCoy 2018; frame the 99.95% as the researched figure), female choice driving it. Keep courtship as sexual-selection ecology. One wonder per rung.

name: Club-winged manakin
scope: T1 recognition of the small red-capped South American forest bird; the headline: the male SINGS WITH HIS WINGS — he rubs two specially thickened wing feathers together over 100 times a second (stridulation, like a cricket) to make a pure violin-like tone, the only bird known to make sound this way; the feathers are so modified that even the FEMALES have solid, dense wing bones (a rare case of a display trait reshaping the whole species' skeleton); the wing-feathers vibrate so fast the trick works better than a syrinx could.
source: References on Machaeropterus deliciosus (wing-feather stridulation ~100+ Hz oscillation, Bostwick & Prum; solid wing bones in both sexes).
framing_note: Anchor = the club-winged manakin. Lead with 'the bird that plays its wings like a violin.' Distinct rungs: wing stridulation sound-making (headline), the resulting solid wing bones even in females (a startling knock-on — a display cost paid across the whole species). Mini depth — thin beats fabricated; two coherent wonders plus the T1 hook. Accuracy: cite Bostwick & Prum; state as the mechanism researchers documented.

name: Sword-billed hummingbird
scope: T1 recognition of the Andean hummingbird with the absurdly long straight bill; the headline: it is the ONLY bird whose bill is longer than the rest of its body — the bill can exceed ~10 cm on a bird whose body is shorter, evolved to reach nectar deep inside long trumpet-shaped Passiflora flowers no other bird can drain (coevolution); because the bill is so long it cannot preen with it, so it uses its FEET to groom instead; it perches with the bill tilted up to balance the weight; the flower and the bird are a matched pair, each shaping the other.
source: References on Ensifera ensifera (bill longer than body — unique, Passiflora coevolution, foot-preening due to bill length, upright bill-carrying posture).
framing_note: Anchor = the sword-billed hummingbird. Lead with 'the only bird with a bill longer than its body.' Distinct rungs: bill-longer-than-body + Passiflora coevolution (headline), the foot-preening consequence (it can't reach itself with the bill — a delightful distinct wonder), the tilted-up carrying posture. One wonder per rung.

name: Hoopoe
scope: T1 recognition of the pinkish-brown crested bird that fans a Mohawk-like crown; the headline defense: the nesting female and chicks smell revolting — the female's preen gland switches to producing a foul, rotten-meat-smelling secretion she smears on her feathers to repel predators and parasites, and the chicks can also spray liquid feces at intruders; the fan-open crest raised in alarm and display; the down-curved bill probing soil for insect grubs; its undulating butterfly-like flight.
source: References on Upupa epops (preen-gland antimicrobial/foul secretion in nesting females, Martín-Vivaldi et al.; chick feces-spraying defense; crest; probing bill).
framing_note: Anchor = the hoopoe. Lead with the stink defense (the beautiful crest is the recognition hook, the smell is the shock). Distinct rungs: the foul preen-gland secretion (headline), the chick feces-spray (a distinct second defense), the fan-crest + probing bill can share the recognition rungs. Mini depth. One wonder per rung.

name: Marabou stork
scope: T1 recognition of the huge, grim, bald-headed African stork (the 'undertaker bird'); the headline: it has one of the largest wingspans of any land bird (up to ~3.7 m), rivaling the biggest, and soars like a vulture; the dangling pink throat pouch is an inflatable air sac connected to its nostrils, used in display and to help it stay cool, NOT a food storage crop as it looks; the bald head and neck are hygiene adaptations for scavenging carcasses like a vulture; it swallows astonishing things whole and follows grass fires to snatch fleeing animals.
source: References on Leptoptilos crumenifer (very large wingspan, inflatable throat air sac function, bald scavenging head, fire-following foraging).
framing_note: Anchor = the marabou stork. Lead with the enormous wingspan (a constructed comparison number is fine — one of the biggest of any land bird). Distinct rungs: giant wingspan (headline), the throat air-sac (correcting the 'it's a food pouch' misread — a teachable accuracy rung), the vulture-like bald scavenging head, fire-following. One wonder per rung; don't restate 'big ugly stork.'
